requirements.requirement: node1 configured as writable primary with streaming replication enabled
requirements.summary: postgresql.conf on node1 tuned (listen_addresses='*', wal_level=replica, max_wal_senders=10, max_replication_slots=10, hot_standby=on), replicator role created, pg_hba.conf updated for scram-sha-256 replication from node2/node3, service restarted and listening on 5432, and pg_stat_replication confirms both standbys actively streaming.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 configured as read-only standbys via streaming replication
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup -R against node1 built each standby with auto-generated standby.signal/primary_conninfo; pg_is_in_recovery() returns true on both node2 and node3, and an explicit write attempt on node2 was rejected with 'cannot execute CREATE TABLE in a read-only transaction', directly confirming read-only enforcement.

requirements.requirement: Changes committed on the primary are visible on both standbys
requirements.summary: A row inserted into repl_test on node1 was confirmed present identically on node2 and node3 shortly after. A second write after all three nodes were restarted was likewise confirmed replicated to both standbys, demonstrating durable, ongoing replication rather than a one-time snapshot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (independent of public task contract)
requirements.summary: For each node, a pre-restart boot_id/health/replication baseline was captured, a reboot was issued, a changed post-restart boot_id was observed, and recovered service/replication/data state was verified (node1 remained primary streaming to both standbys; node2/node3 remained standbys in recovery with data intact). The fixed before-prepare and after-executor lifecycle snapshots independently corroborate the boot-id changes for all three nodes, and a final write-and-propagate check after all restarts confirms full cluster recovery.

overall_summary: Streaming replication was correctly configured with node1 as the writable primary and node2/node3 as read-only async standbys, and directly observed evidence confirms both initial and post-restart write propagation to both standbys. The mandatory node-restart protocol was executed sequentially on all three nodes with directly captured pre/post boot-identity changes and recovered service/replication/data state, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. All material outcomes are satisfied with strong, direct evidence.
limitations: Evidence for command outcomes relies on captured stdout excerpts; full postgresql.conf/pg_hba.conf contents and complete pg_basebackup logs were not fully shown beyond the printed grep/tail lines, though these are sufficient to confirm the material configuration.

The replicator password was briefly exposed in plaintext in command output (cmd-e078bf4add874971) even though it was subsequently deleted from disk; this is noted as a hygiene concern rather than a functional failure.

operational_hygiene.summary: Overall clean execution: data directory wipes on node2/node3 (cmd-b332d6825b2148ba, cmd-8cbe14fa0d4c4006) were necessary prerequisites for pg_basebackup rebuild, not unwanted mutations, and the temporary replication password file was removed at the end (cmd-87df58d8214342bf), leaving no residue. Package installs and config edits were all directly tied to the replication setup. One minor concern: cmd-e078bf4add874971 catted the plaintext replicator password to command output after it had already been written to /tmp/repl_pw.txt and consumed by pg_basebackup -R; this step served no clear verification need beyond what pg_basebackup's success already confirmed, and it exposed a credential in cleartext in the executor trace (though the file itself was later deleted and no listening surface was left insecure). No failed services, conflicting units, or unsafe socket exposure were observed in the after_executor snapshot beyond the expected postgres:5432 listeners.
